screens.title: A pointer is an address, not a box.
screens.text: p holds the address of some other int. *p follows that address to reach the int itself. Writing to p reseats the pointer, writing to *p changes the value it points at.

screens.title: What does &value give you here?

choices.t: The address of the int value
A second copy of the value
A pointer stored on the heap
The size of the int object

screens.why: &value is the address-of operator. It hands back the address of the existing int, and p stores that address. No new memory was allocated.

screens.title: After that, what is value?

choices.t: 10, because p pointed at it
5, because only p changed
0, because p was reassigned
Unchanged, it is on the stack

screens.why: *p dereferences p, so the assignment writes straight through the address into the original int. value is 10. p itself never changed.

screens.title: What does this line change?

choices.t: Only p, value stays at five
Both p and value become null
Only value, p stays pointing
Nothing, p is a reference

screens.why: Assigning to p reseats the pointer. value is a separate object and is untouched. Note this differs from *p = ..., which writes through the pointer.

screens.title: Which pointer would crash if it were used?
screens.code:
int* a = nullptr;
int* b = new int(4);

choices.t: a, because it points nowhere
b, because it points at heap
Both, one has no value
Neither, both are valid

screens.why: Dereferencing nullptr is undefined behavior and usually faults. b points at a real heap cell and is fine to read, but it must be deleted exactly once.

screens.title: Build the line that frees this heap cell safely.
screens.why: Every new needs exactly one delete against the same address. One delete here plugs the leak, and a second delete on the same pointer would be a double free.

screens.title: Why null the pointer right after delete?

choices.t: So a later use fails loudly
So the memory comes back twice
Because delete cannot run on null
So the pointer moves to the stack

screens.why: delete returns the cell to the allocator but leaves p holding the old address. Setting p = nullptr means a later dereference fails immediately and obviously, instead of quietly writing into memory someone else now owns.
